records.text: Story points are becoming outdated for AI-driven development. When your team is made of AI agents, I think we need a different way to understand the work. Instead of asking only: “How many story points did we complete?” I want to see: → how many tokens were spent → how much machine time was used → what actually progressed → where agents are blocked → how much work is waiting for a human That is why I built a local Kanban into my Claude Code telemetry dashboard. I use it as a real-time operational view of my AI team. The Kanban itself is deliberately simple: BACKLOG → IN PROGRESS → BLOCKED → REVIEW → DONE Each task is connected to the existing telemetry, so I can see the agent, project, branch, duration, tokens, output, weighted usage and machine time without duplicating the data. But the real value for me is not the Kanban itself. It is the combination of two very different information layers. Confluence is the knowledge and decision layer. That is where I keep: → project goals and context → questions that require my input → decisions and decision tracking → results and findings → documentation produced by the agents Agents periodically write there, and I work with that information asynchronously. The dashboard is the operational layer. It gives me a real-time picture of what the AI team is doing right now: → which tasks are running → which agents are working → what is blocked → what is waiting for review → how much machine time and tokens are being consumed So I don’t need to constantly jump between Claude sessions to understand what is happening. I can work asynchronously through Confluence while keeping the real-time operational picture in the dashboard. And this is where I find the combination particularly useful. For example, a task might have been “IN PROGRESS” for three hours, but the actual machine time could be only 40 minutes. That shows me that the remaining time was spent waiting, for another agent, a dependency, or me. The key when working with an AI team is to pay close attention not just to agent activity, but to how efficiently the team produces a real, deliverable outcome. For example: • for customer pipeline optimization - the number and quality of ready-to-send recommendations that can be directly shared with the customer; • for an AI bug-fixer - the number of successfully fixed bugs relative to the number of tokens consumed; • for any other workflow - define a specific, measurable outcome and evaluate it against the AI resources consumed.

records.text: Dal 18 al 20 settembre il Politecnico di Milano ha aperto le porte al pubblico per il Festival Internazionale dell’Ingegneria 2026, dedicato quest’anno al tema “Technology for Humanity”. Anche il Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano ha partecipato al Festival portando ricerca e ingegneria aerospaziale fuori dai laboratori e a contatto con il pubblico. Tra open labs, lezioni divulgative e attività dedicate a bambini e teenager, i visitatori hanno potuto scoprire da vicino alcune delle sfide su cui lavorano ogni giorno i nostri ricercatori: dall’esplorazione e dalla sostenibilità nello spazio ai satelliti e ai detriti orbitali, dai materiali avanzati alle strutture aeronautiche del futuro, fino all’energia eolica, all’aeroacustica, alla sicurezza dei veicoli e alle nuove soluzioni per un’aviazione più efficiente. Un’occasione per aprire i nostri laboratori, mostrare tecnologie e prototipi e raccontare la ricerca attraverso esperimenti, dimostrazioni e attività interattive rivolte a pubblici di tutte le età. records.text: Reliable drone performance depends on more than the airframe. Materials play a critical role in protecting sensitive electronics, supporting communication components and maintaining performance in changing outdoor conditions. Trinseo material solutions can help manufacturers address key requirements across drone components, including: ✔ Signal transmission for communication components ✔ Impact resistance for protective housings ✔ Dimensional stability for precise component fit ✔ UV and weather resistance for outdoor operation ✔ Flame-retardant options for demanding applications From battery enclosures and upper covers to remote controllers and optical components, Trinseo helps manufacturers select materials designed to support reliable performance across critical drone systems.

records.text: 🎥 Tour diary: Salinas. Every tour has a stop that just feels different. For Midnight, that was this past weekend flying for the crowd in Salinas - the airport that's played home to our flight test program for the past several years. For the second year running, Midnight took to the sky at the California International Air Show, sharing the bill with the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds, Goulian Aerosports, and a lineup of icons including the MiG-17, T-33, and A-37 Dragonfly. Hundreds of Archer team members turned out to enjoy the show with the community that's been with us from day one. The "No Roads" Flight Tour continues to San Jose, Oakland, San Francisco, Los Angeles and beyond.

records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or gov
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, n
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA

records.text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors perfor

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano put it plainly: CAML gives the Army "a pathway to experiment with modular launcher concepts, learn quickly, and make informed decisions at the speed of relevance." Still prototype-stage, no production commitment — which means the interface architecture is exactly what's being tested right now. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #MOSA
